rationale: The plasma samples come from two acquisition batches, and Astral DIA runs often shift protein levels by batch. Those shifts can hide the disease signal or be mistaken for it. I'm adding one change: after per-sample median centring, each protein is centred on its own batch median. This uses only batch metadata and no labels, so the model sees differences between people rather than batch offsets.

In plasma DIA data, whether a protein is detected at all depends on how abundant it is. Proteins detected in only 20–80% of samples are currently thrown away by the 70% presence filter or blurred by half-min imputation. This change adds their detected/not-detected flags as a separate, down-weighted feature block. Each flag is centred on its own batch's training-set detection rate so batch differences in depth don't pass for disease signal.

Plasma proteomes are often contaminated by red blood cells (from hemolysis) and platelets (from handling before centrifugation). This adds sample-specific variation that has nothing to do with disease and can swamp the small Alzheimer's signal at n=89. In `featurize`, I build an erythrocyte score and a platelet score for each sample from established marker panels (Geyer et al. 2019). Each protein's observed log values are then regressed on both scores and only the slope part is removed. This step uses no labels, keeps each protein's mean, and leaves the rest of the pipeline unchanged.

With n=89, a uniform L2 penalty treats all ~2–3k retained proteins as equally likely to carry signal. That dilutes the coefficients of proteins already linked to Alzheimer's in plasma, CSF and brain: APOE/CLU, the complement cascade, neuronal and glial injury markers (NEFL/GFAP/YWHAG), the SMOC1/SPP1/CHI3L1 module, synaptic proteins and inflammation/lipid-transport proteins. This change adds a Bayesian-style informative prior by scaling those standardized features up by 2×, which cuts their effective penalty by 4×. Everything else is unchanged, and the change uses no labels.

Geyer et al. (2019) describe three plasma quality-marker panels, and I only use two (erythrocyte and platelet). This change adds the third: coagulation/partial clotting, measured with fibrinogen chains and Factor XIII. These proteins vary with pre-analytical clotting, not disease. I'll regress their axis out of each protein in the same label-free, slope-only way. That should remove another source of sample-handling noise that the L2 model at n=89 could otherwise fit.

Remove protein groups for immunoglobulin variable regions (IGHV/IGKV/IGLV and similar) from both the intensity block and the missingness-indicator block. Their levels and detection depend on each person's antibody repertoire rather than Alzheimer's biology. They are often detected in 20–80% of samples, so they flood the indicator block with person-specific noise that an L2 model at n=89 can overfit.

With n=89, a few extreme plasma values (acute-phase spikes, lipaemic samples, odd values left after imputation) can take over the L2 logistic regression's coefficients and decision scores, especially for the up-weighted prior proteins. This change caps every standardized intensity feature at ±3 SD, using the training-fold scaler, before the prior weighting. Extreme samples still count, but no single one can dominate. No labels are used. I have not run this; its effect on the dev score is unknown.

At n=89, each known AD plasma protein measured on its own is noisy. Averaging the standardized proteins within each biological module (complement, lipid transport/APOE-CLU, neuronal/glial injury, the SMOC1/SPP1 matrisome module, acute-phase inflammation, glycolysis) should give a few higher signal-to-noise pathway scores. I append these as a small block of extra features with the same up-weighting as the prior proteins; everything else stays the same, and no labels are used.

Right now the batch correction only removes each protein's median shift between batches. But Astral DIA batches also differ in dynamic range, so a protein can be more spread out in one batch than the other. The pooled StandardScaler and the L2 model then give the noisier batch more leverage, and that difference can look like disease signal. I'm adding a ComBat-style scale step that uses no labels. Within each batch, each protein's robust spread (MAD) is rescaled to its pooled spread. The log ratio is shrunk toward 1, more strongly for small batches, so small-n noise isn't amplified. I haven't run this, so its effect on the dev score is unknown.

With about 3,000 features and n=89, the L2 logistic regression estimates every coefficient jointly, so its weights pick up noisy correlations between proteins. A diagonal (naive-Bayes-style) discriminant ignores those correlations, which is known to be more stable when there are far more features than samples (Bickel & Levina). This change adds a shrunken diagonal-LDA score built on the same feature matrix and averages it with the LR score, after putting both on a common scale using training-fold statistics only. The aim is to cut the variance of the final ranking without adding any tuned hyperparameters. I haven't run it, so its effect on the dev score is unknown.

Right now each sample is centred on the median of whichever proteins happened to be detected in it. In DIA plasma data, missing values are mostly low-abundance proteins, so a shallower run has a higher observed median and all of its values get pushed down. Centring each sample on the median of a fixed core set of proteins detected in at least 95% of samples should remove that bias, which comes from detection depth rather than disease. The step uses no labels and nothing else in the pipeline changes. I haven't run it, so its effect on the dev score is unknown.

Low-abundance brain-derived AD markers in plasma, such as NEFL, GFAP, YWHAG, SMOC1, NPTX2 and SPP1, are usually quantified in only 20–80% of samples. They fail the 70% presence filter, so the 2× prior up-weighting never reaches them; they only appear as plain detection flags. Detection depends on abundance, so a detected flag mostly means the protein is elevated. This change applies the same prior weight to the detection flags of known AD proteins, so their evidence counts as intended. It uses no labels.

The L2 strength C=0.05 was fixed by hand, but the best amount of shrinkage at n≈71 per training fold depends on the feature set that is now in use (prior up-weighting, clipping, indicator block). This change picks C from a small grid inside each training fold, using repeated stratified grouped inner CV that rebuilds the whole fold-specific design (filtering, imputation, scaling, indicators) in every inner split. Ties go to the stronger penalty, and no outer-fold information is used. I haven't run this, so its effect on the dev score is unknown.

Low-abundance, brain- or glia-derived plasma AD markers (e.g. GFAP, NEFL, YWHAG, SMOC1, SPP1, CHI3L1) are often quantified in only 50–70% of Astral plasma runs. The 70% presence filter currently drops their intensities, so the model sees only a binary detection flag and the 2× prior weight never applies to them. This change lowers the intensity-block presence threshold to 50% so their measured levels enter the model. Half-min imputation is kept, so non-detection, which here means low abundance, still reads as a low value. Nothing else changes and no labels are used. I haven't run this, so its effect on the dev score is unknown.

Detection of the 20–80%-present proteins mostly reflects how deep each run went (peptide load, instrument sensitivity), so the detection-flag block is dominated by one shared depth axis that has nothing to do with Alzheimer's. This change estimates each sample's batch-centred detection depth from the flags themselves and removes it from every flag using the training-fold slope. It uses no labels and leaves only the protein-specific detection patterns. I haven't run it, so its effect on the dev score is unknown.

Clipping at ±3 SD gave a gain, which suggests a few heavy-tailed values are pushing the n=89 L2 model around. Acute-phase spikes, lipaemia and leftover imputation artefacts can do that even on the log scale. This change replaces z-scoring plus clipping with a rank-based inverse-normal transform of each protein, fitted on the training fold only. Test samples are mapped through the training fold's empirical quantiles, so each protein is pushed toward a Gaussian shape and no single sample can dominate. Half-min-imputed non-detections become tied lowest ranks, so they still read as low abundance. No labels are used. I haven't run this, so its effect on the dev score is unknown.

The current prior list is mostly CSF and brain markers. Many of those, such as NEFL, GFAP, SMOC1 and NPTX2, are rarely quantified above the 70% threshold in plasma. Meanwhile, plasma-MS AD studies repeatedly report another set: acute-phase and inter-alpha-trypsin inhibitors (ITIH1–4, AHSG, AFM, LRG1, ORM), gelsolin, HDL/lipoprotein proteins (PON1, APOM, APOB, APOC3), other complement factors (CFHR, C6–C8, CD5L) and fibrinogen/kininogen. The round-5 drop after removing the clotting axis suggests these proteins carry signal here. I'm adding these well-quantified plasma proteins as a second, milder prior tier (weight 1.5, so about 2.25× less effective L2 penalty), with no labels and no tuning.

Removing the erythrocyte and platelet contamination axes from the protein intensities was one of the largest gains so far (round 3), but those axes were never removed from the detection-flag block. Whether low-abundance red-cell and platelet proteins are detected at all depends on hemolysis and pre-centrifugation handling, not on Alzheimer's. This change carries each sample's two contamination scores (computed without labels in `featurize`) through to `fit_predict`. There, each batch-centred detection flag is regressed on the scores within the training fold, and only that training-fold slope is removed from both training and test flags. I have not run this, so its effect on the dev score is unknown.

DIA-NN plasma output often has several protein groups for the same gene (isoforms, fragments, and so on; ambiguous `A;B` groups are kept separate). Each copy is penalized on its own in the L2 model, so a gene with more copies gets more total influence for technical reasons. This change averages the training-fold Gaussianized features that share the same gene key into one feature per gene before scaling, so each gene counts once. It uses no labels, and groups with no gene name are left as they are.

The label-free per-batch median centring will remove real disease signal if the two batches hold different proportions of AD cases. This change re-estimates each protein's batch offset inside the training fold with diagnosis as a protected covariate (ComBat-style protein ~ batch + diagnosis, using the training fold's labels only) and subtracts only the batch term from training and test samples, which corrects batch differences without erasing class differences. I haven't run this, so its effect on the dev score is unknown.
